newsitem.title: USA: Florida tobacco case brings threats, protection for jurors.
newsitem.headline: Florida tobacco case brings threats, protection for jurors.

text.p: The judge in Florida's billion-dollar lawsuit against the tobacco industry on Friday barred news organizations from publishing pictures of prospective jurors.
Judge Harold Cohen issued his order just moments before the start of jury selection in the landmark trial -- the first lawsuit brought by a state against the industry to go to trial.
Cohen said he was concerned that if photographs or video of jurors' faces were published, someone might recognize them and try to influence their thinking.

"They (the public) might harass or interfere with the judicial process," Cohen said, adding that he felt the court had the right to do whatever was necessary to protect jurors during a trial that could last into January.
The judge also said there were possible safety concerns regarding the jury.

"There have been threats to lawyers, there have been crank calls and crank mail to the courts," Cohen said in announcing his ruling to a group of attorneys and state officials that included Gov. Lawton Chiles and Attorney General Bob Butterworth.
Some 300 prospective jurors were assembled, from which six jurors and nine alternates will be selected for trial. Florida is seeking to recover its cost for treating sick smokers.

W.C. Gentry, one of Florida's lawyers, said tobacco companies already had launched a campaign to bring pressure by convenience stores and other businesses that stand to lose money if cigarette sales drop.
"If jurors faces are published, they might be recognized when they shop at these stores. People will speak to them. They can't have a private life," Gentry said.
Justus Reid, an attorney for Lorillard Tobacco Co., told Reuters that a law firm involved in the case had received threats.
He declined to name the firm but said it "has taken this threat seriously enough to alter the scheduling of attorney movements."
